processing: A versatile early-budding cultivar rather than a single style: it has been made into black tea, green tea, baozhong and Taiwanese Tieguanyin. Today it is best known in charcoal-roasted Tieguanyin from Shimen.
harvest_season: An early-budding cultivar, so it starts ahead of later varieties in spring. Picking calendars vary by producer and little is documented about which picking is most prized.
appearance_dry: Large leaf; in the Shimen Tieguanyin style, typically dark, tightly rolled pellets, as with other roasted ball-rolled oolongs.
appearance_liquor: In roasted Tieguanyin style, typically a clear amber, as with other roasted Taiwanese oolongs; the colour depends on what the leaf was made into.
appearance_wet: Large, thick-looking leaves that open out after a few steeps, darkened by the roast in the Tieguanyin style.
taste_profile: Few tasting descriptions exist for the cultivar itself. Shimen's Tieguanyin is known for a particular aroma from longan charcoal roasting, so expect roast and warm wood, as with other charcoal-fired oolongs.

brewing.notes: Advice for the roasted Tieguanyin style, the usual way to meet this cultivar. Green or black teas from the same leaf need gentler treatment.

vintage_note: Not sold under one fixed scheme, since the name is a cultivar. Roasted Shimen Tieguanyin is typically sold like other charcoal-fired oolongs, by harvest season of the current or a recent year, and it holds up better than unroasted tea. Ask the seller which harvest and when it was roasted.
description:
Ying Zhi Hong Xin is a large-leaved, early-budding Taiwanese tea cultivar, brought over from Fujian during the Qing period and also called Da Guang Hong Xin. You will rarely see the name on a label, yet it matters twice over: as the leaf behind Shimen Tieguanyin, and as a parent of two of Taiwan's modern cultivars.

It is an unusually flexible leaf. It has gone into export black and green teas, into baozhong, and into Tieguanyin, which is normally associated with a different cultivar. The growing area today centres on Tamsui and Shimen on the north coast of New Taipei.

Descriptions of how the cultivar itself tastes are scarce, so judge the tea by its style. The Shimen version is charcoal-roasted over longan wood, and like other roasted oolongs it wants water near the boil and benefits from a few steeps to show its sweetness under the roast.

When buying, look for Shimen Tieguanyin and ask about the cultivar, because shops rarely volunteer it. If you drink Jin Xuan, trying this one is a neat way to taste part of its family tree.
history:
The cultivar came to Taiwan from Fujian during Qing rule. Under Japanese rule it was ranked among the island's four main tea varieties and was grown widely, mostly for export black and green tea. Those four varieties also served as the genetic base for early breeding work. After 1945 it went into baozhong sold as red-water baozhong.

In the 1980s the Shimen farmers' association, with guidance from the tea research station, began making Tieguanyin from it, and in 1991 it moved from electric roasting to hand roasting over longan charcoal. Its breeding legacy includes Jin Xuan and Cui Yu, both named in 1981.
